body.heading: Lifted by the Sun
paragraphs: The Sun evaporates water from oceans, lakes, soil and leaves — plants release vast quantities through transpiration — and the vapour rises into the atmosphere. Cooling as it climbs, it condenses into cloud droplets and eventually falls as precipitation. Some rain runs off into rivers; some soaks into groundwater; some locks into ice. All of it, eventually, returns to the sea or the sky to go around again.

The amounts are staggering. The atmosphere holds only about two weeks' worth of the planet's water at any moment, constantly exchanged. A water molecule spends, on average, about nine days in the air, a few weeks in a river, thousands of years in deep groundwater — and around 3,000 years in the ocean.

body.heading: A cycle with no beginning
paragraphs: Earth's water is essentially a closed account: almost none arrives or leaves. The water dinosaurs drank is the water in today's rain. What changes is only where it sits — ocean, ice cap, aquifer, cloud — and those storages are the buffers of the whole system.

That is why the water cycle is also a story about care. Pollution put into a river enters a loop that returns to taps, fields and seas. The cycle forgives nothing and forgets nothing; it simply keeps everything moving.

takeaway: The water cycle endlessly circulates Earth's fixed supply of water through ocean, air, land and ice.
